transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Anytime I have to get on the freeway, I go out of my way to avoid it or white-knuckle my way through the drive, and it’s gotten to the point where it’s really disrupting my routine. I'm just hoping to get some help with managing this.
Can you tell me more about what specifically happens or what you experience when you're driving on the freeway that makes it so distressing for you?

Even just seeing a freeway sign makes my heart pound and my hands get clammy with this wave of pure dread. When I'm actually driving, I grip the wheel so hard my knuckles hurt, hold my breath whenever a truck passes, and feel convinced I'm going to die. It gets so bad that I sometimes start shaking uncontrollably and have to pull off at the next exit.
Do you experience these intense fear or panic symptoms in situations other than driving on the freeway, or is it primarily related to freeway driving?

No, it is strictly tied to the freeway. I feel completely fine driving on local side streets and in other areas of my life. The panic only kicks in when I see freeway signs, plan a route that includes them, or actually have to get on the highway.
Can you think of any particular incident or experience related to freeway driving that might have triggered this intense fear for you?

Yes, about seven months ago, I was driving home on the 210 after a hike in the San Gabriel Mountains when a truck lost a ladder, causing a terrible multi-car pileup right in front of me. Witnessing that chaotic scene with shattered glass and first responders rescuing people completely shook me. Ever since that crash, my brain has been absolutely terrified of getting back on the freeway.

Did you experience any symptoms of persistent and pervasive distress, such as flashbacks, nightmares, or avoidance of reminders, beyond just the fear of driving on the freeway, after witnessing the accident?

No, I don't experience nightmares or flashbacks when I'm at home or sleeping, and my avoidance is strictly limited to the freeway itself. That wave of dread like I'm back in the pileup only happens when I see a freeway on-ramp or look at GPS directions that include the highway. It never just happens randomly out of nowhere.
Can you describe how you felt immediately after the accident, and did you experience any intense fear, helplessness, or horror in response to what happened?

It was absolutely horrifying; even though I wasn't physically hurt, watching first responders extract a crying child from a crumpled SUV amidst screeching brakes and shattered glass left a deep impression. I felt an intense wave of dread and helplessness in that moment. Now, that same terrifying panic washes over me with a pounding heart and clammy hands whenever I even get near a freeway.

You mentioned the accident and your subsequent fear of driving on the freeway, but can you tell me if you've been experiencing any significant distress or impairment in other areas of your life, such as work, relationships, or daily activities, beyond just the freeway driving?

Yes, it has really disrupted my life. I've been late to work trainings, which led to my principal confronting me, and I've completely stopped going to my hiking group and salsa classes. I've even started skipping family gatherings, and now my parents are constantly questioning why I'm not showing up anymore.

Do you ever have unwanted memories or thoughts about the accident that aren't triggered by seeing freeway signs or driving, or are your distressing memories and feelings strictly tied to the act of driving on the freeway or seeing related cues?

No, I don't really get those thoughts or memories out of the blue when I'm away from those triggers. They are strictly tied to seeing freeway signs, looking at GPS routes, or being near big trucks. When I'm completely away from anything related to the freeway, my mind is totally at ease.
